Epidemiology & Risk Factors.title: Epidemiology & Risk Factors in Head & Neck Cancer
Epidemiology & Risk Factors.html:
Head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) is not one disease but a family of cancers arising from the mucosal lining of the mouth, throat, and voice box, and the risk factors that cause it differ sharply by subsite. Understanding who gets these cancers and why is the foundation for everything else, it explains why an oropharynx patient in 2026 looks so different from one in 1990, and why nasopharyngeal cancer is treated as its own category entirely.

How Common Is Each Subsite?

The oral cavity and the oropharynx are by far the two largest contributors to HNSCC. Oral cavity cancer accounts for about 30% of head and neck malignancies, and the oropharynx is the single most common head and neck subsite overall, at just over 30%. Both are overwhelmingly squamous cell carcinoma (95% for oral cavity, >90% for oropharynx). Laryngeal cancer is also common and skews heavily male; roughly two-thirds of laryngeal cancers arise in the glottis (true vocal cords), about one-third in the supraglottis, and only 1–2% in the subglottis. Nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC), by contrast, is rare in the United States (0.5–2 per 100,000) but is endemic in southern China, Southeast Asia, and North Africa, where incidence can reach roughly 25 per 100,000: a difference large enough that it points to a fundamentally different set of causes.

Oral Cavity: The Classic Tobacco-and-Alcohol Cancer

Oral cavity cancer is driven largely by direct mucosal exposure to carcinogens and chronic irritation. Smoking, alcohol, and chewing (smokeless) tobacco are the dominant risk factors and often act together. Betel nut chewing is a major risk factor as well. Chronic local irritation matters here in a way it doesn't for most other subsites, poor oral hygiene, periodontal disease, and ill-fitting dentures rubbing against mucosa over years can promote malignant change, and lip cancer specifically is linked to chronic sun exposure. Immunosuppression (HIV, solid organ transplant) and rare inherited bone-marrow-failure syndromes (Fanconi anemia, dyskeratosis congenita) are less common but important contributors. Many oral cavity cancers arise from a visible precursor lesion called leukoplakia, a white mucosal patch that carries roughly a 1–20% risk of transforming into invasive cancer over 10 years, which is why any nonhealing white or red oral lesion deserves biopsy rather than reassurance.

Oropharynx: Two Diseases Wearing One Name

This is the subsite where epidemiology has changed the most. Historically, oropharyngeal cancer looked just like oral cavity cancer, an older, heavy smoker/drinker with a keratinizing squamous tumor. Over the past few decades a second, biologically distinct disease has become dominant: HPV-associated oropharyngeal cancer. The two present in almost mirror-image demographics.

HPV-positiveHPV-negative
AgeYoungerOlder
Smoking/alcoholNon/light smokerHeavy smoker and drinker
RaceCaucasianNon-Caucasian
Other risk factorHigh-risk sexual behaviorNot linked to sexual behavior
Favored subsiteTonsil / base of tongueNo particular preference
HistologyNonkeratinizing, basaloid, poorly differentiatedKeratinizing
Molecular driverp16 upregulatedp53 mutation, EGFR amplified

The biology behind this is worth knowing because it explains how HPV status is actually tested. High-risk HPV produces two viral oncoproteins, E6 and E7. E7 binds and inactivates the retinoblastoma protein (pRb), which normally restrains the cell cycle; this deregulates proliferation and, as a downstream consequence, causes p16, a cell-cycle inhibitor that pRb normally keeps suppressed, to become markedly overexpressed. E6 binds and degrades p53, disabling the cell's main tumor-suppressor checkpoint. Because p16 overexpression is easy to detect by immunohistochemistry and tracks HPV infection with roughly 95% concordance, p16 positivity is used clinically as a surrogate marker for HPV-driven disease.

Why This Distinction Changed the Field

HPV-positive oropharyngeal cancer has a substantially better prognosis than HPV-negative disease, stage for stage, these patients tend to respond better to chemoradiation and have higher cure rates, even though they may present with more extensive nodal disease. This prognostic gap is large enough that the AJCC 8th edition staging system now stages HPV-positive and HPV-negative oropharyngeal cancer as two entirely separate diseases, with different (and generally more favorable) group-stage groupings for HPV-positive tumors. This single epidemiologic shift, a virus creating a younger, healthier, better-prognosis population, is the reason so much modern research asks whether these patients can be treated less intensively without sacrificing cure rates, a theme picked up again in the Treatment Paradigms and High-Yield Literature documents.

Nasopharynx: A Virus- and Geography-Driven Cancer

NPC's epidemiology is dominated by a single virus and a distinctive geographic and dietary pattern. Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) is detectable in nearly 95% of endemic cases and over 20% of non-endemic cases. Traditional dietary exposures linked to endemic regions, salt-preserved fish, other preserved foods, and a low fruit/vegetable diet, along with tobacco smoke, family history, and (in non-endemic, keratinizing disease) HPV round out the risk factor list. Endemic NPC is overwhelmingly the nonkeratinizing, undifferentiated histologic subtype (WHO type III), which is also the subtype with the most favorable prognosis, while the U.S. sees relatively more of the keratinizing subtype.

Clinical PearlHPV-positive and HPV-negative oropharyngeal cancer should be thought of as two different diseases occurring at the same anatomic site, different patient, different biology, different staging system, and (stage for stage) different prognosis. Always know a patient's p16/HPV status before discussing prognosis or treatment intensity.
Clinical PearlA persistent oral leukoplakia is not "just irritation", it is a premalignant lesion with a real (1–20% over 10 years) risk of transformation into invasive squamous cell carcinoma and warrants biopsy.

Anatomy & Lymphatics.title: Head & Neck Anatomy & the Lymph Node Level System
Anatomy & Lymphatics.html:
Radiation oncology in the head and neck is fundamentally an exercise in geography: knowing exactly which structures a tumor can invade, and exactly which lymph nodes it is likely to spread to, determines how a treatment field is drawn. This document covers the two anatomic frameworks you need cold, the subsite anatomy of the major disease sites, and the cervical lymph node level system (levels I–VII) that every head and neck radiation plan is built around.

Oral Cavity: Seven Subsites, One Important Boundary

The oral cavity extends from the lips to the point where the mouth becomes the throat, and is divided into seven subsites: the lip, gingiva/alveolar ridges, oral tongue (specifically the anterior two-thirds, the posterior third, or base of tongue, belongs to the oropharynx), floor of mouth, buccal mucosa, retromolar trigone (the small triangular area behind the last lower molar), and hard palate. The line between "anterior two-thirds tongue" and "posterior one-third tongue (base of tongue)" is a favorite testable boundary, because a tumor that seems to be "just tongue cancer" is staged and managed completely differently depending on which side of that line it sits.

Oropharynx and Nasopharynx: Defined by Their Neighbors

The oropharynx sits directly behind the oral cavity and contains four subsites: base of tongue, palatine tonsils, soft palate, and posterior pharyngeal wall. Its boundaries are defined relative to visible landmarks: anteriorly the circumvallate papillae and anterior tonsillar pillars, superiorly the soft palate, inferiorly the vallecula and tip of the epiglottis, and laterally the tonsillar fossae and pillars.

The nasopharynx sits above and behind the oropharynx, at the very top of the pharyngeal tube, bounded anteriorly by the posterior nasal septum/posterior nares, posteriorly by the C1–C2 vertebrae, superiorly by the skull base, inferiorly by the soft palate, and laterally by the eustachian tube opening, torus tubarius, and the fossa of Rosenmüller: a small mucosal recess that is, importantly, the site of origin of most nasopharyngeal carcinomas.

The Larynx: Three Compartments, Three Very Different Personalities

The larynx is divided into three vertically stacked compartments, and the boundaries between them matter enormously because each compartment behaves like a different disease. The supraglottis runs from the tip of the epiglottis down to the laryngeal ventricle and includes the epiglottis, false vocal cords, arytenoids, and aryepiglottic folds. The glottis is the true vocal cords plus the anterior and posterior commissures. The subglottis extends from the undersurface of the true cords down to the inferior border of the cricoid cartilage. Roughly two-thirds of laryngeal cancers arise in the glottis, about one-third in the supraglottis, and only 1–2% in the subglottis.

The single most important functional fact about laryngeal anatomy is that the glottis has almost no lymphatics, while the supraglottis and subglottis have rich lymphatic networks. This is why early glottic cancer (T1–T2) so rarely spreads to lymph nodes (about 2% for T1, 5% for T2) and can often be treated with radiation to the primary site alone, while supraglottic and subglottic tumors are assumed to be at meaningful risk for occult nodal spread from the outset and are treated with elective neck coverage even when the neck appears clinically negative.

The Cervical Lymph Node Levels: A Shared Language

Nearly every head and neck cancer drains into a predictable set of cervical lymph nodes, and surgeons, radiologists, and radiation oncologists all describe those nodes using the same standardized "level" system (levels I through VII) rather than vague terms like "upper neck." This matters clinically for three reasons: it lets a radiologist describe exactly which nodes are enlarged, it lets a surgeon describe exactly which nodes were removed in a neck dissection, and it lets a radiation oncologist draw an elective (prophylactic) treatment volume that reliably covers the nodes at risk for a given primary tumor without irradiating the entire neck.

LevelRegionKey boundaries
Ia / IbSubmental / SubmandibularSuperior: mylohyoid/mandible. Inferior: hyoid bone. Ia is anteromedial between the digastric muscles; Ib is posterolateral and contains the submandibular gland.
IIUpper jugularSkull base to inferior border of the hyoid bone; IIa lies anterior to the internal jugular vein, IIb posterior to it.
IIIMid jugularInferior hyoid bone to inferior border of the cricoid cartilage.
IVLower jugularInferior cricoid cartilage down to the level of the clavicle.
Va / VbPosterior trianglePosterior to the sternocleidomastoid muscle, skull base to clavicle; Va is superior (includes spinal accessory nodes), Vb is inferior (includes lateral supraclavicular nodes).
VICentral compartmentPretracheal, paratracheal, prelaryngeal (Delphian), and perithyroid nodes; hyoid bone to the suprasternal notch, medial to the carotid arteries.
VIIRetropharyngeal (Rouvière)Behind the pharyngeal wall, in front of the prevertebral fascia, essentially a cranial extension of level II.

How Drainage Predicts What Gets Treated

Because lymphatic drainage from each subsite is fairly predictable, radiation oncologists use "if this subsite, then cover these levels" rules rather than reinventing the nodal target volume for every patient. A few of the most important patterns:

  • Levels II–IV are covered almost always, and almost always bilaterally: the major exceptions are well-lateralized tonsil tumors without base-of-tongue or soft palate involvement, and certain well-lateralized oral cavity tumors, which may be treated with unilateral neck coverage alone.
  • Any tumor of a "pharynx" site (naso-, oro-, or hypopharynx) should have retropharyngeal (level VII) nodes covered.
  • Nasopharynx is unique in routinely requiring coverage of level V as well.
  • Subglottic extension mandates coverage of level VI.
  • Tumors of the lower lip, anterior oral tongue, or anterior floor of mouth require coverage of level Ia; the upper lip instead drains primarily to facial lymphatics rather than level Ia.
  • If a given nodal level is already involved with tumor, the general rule is to extend coverage to the adjacent nodal levels at a lower (elective) dose, for example, an involved level II node prompts low-dose coverage of adjacent levels Ib and V, in addition to full-dose coverage of all of level II.

Oral cavity subsite drainage follows a similarly predictable logic: the lip drains to Ib and II–IV (the lower lip specifically to Ia; the upper lip to facial lymphatics); the oral tongue drains anteriorly to Ia, laterally to Ib, and medially to II–IV; the floor of mouth drains anteriorly to Ia and otherwise to Ib and II–IV; and gingiva, buccal mucosa, retromolar trigone, and hard palate drain primarily to Ib and II–IV.

Clinical PearlThe glottis's sparse lymphatics versus the supraglottis/subglottis's rich lymphatics is one of the most exam-relevant facts in head and neck anatomy: it is the anatomic reason early glottic cancer can skip elective neck treatment entirely while supraglottic and subglottic tumors cannot.
Clinical PearlRetropharyngeal (level VII) nodes should be covered for any pharyngeal primary (naso-, oro-, or hypopharynx), a rule that is easy to forget because these nodes are deep and not palpable on exam.

Workup & Staging.title: Head & Neck Cancer: Workup & Staging
Workup & Staging.html:
Before any treatment decision can be made, every head and neck cancer patient goes through a structured evaluation to define exactly what the tumor is, how far it has spread, and whether the patient can physically tolerate the treatment being considered. This workup feeds directly into AJCC TNM staging, which, unlike many other cancers, is customized subsite by subsite in the head and neck, because the same T-stage number can mean anatomically very different things depending on where the tumor started.

The Core Workup, Common to Every Subsite

Regardless of subsite, the workup starts with a thorough history and physical: visual inspection and palpation of the primary tumor (noting size, location, and mobility/fixation), a full cranial nerve exam, and careful palpation of the cervical lymph nodes. Flexible nasolaryngoscopy is used broadly to inspect mucosal surfaces and screen for a second primary tumor, head and neck cancer patients, especially those with a heavy tobacco history, are at meaningfully increased risk of a second, separate cancer elsewhere in the aerodigestive tract.

Cross-sectional imaging typically includes CT of the neck with contrast to characterize the primary tumor and nodes, CT chest without contrast to screen for pulmonary metastases or a second lung primary, and often PET-CT for nodal and distant staging (PET is generally more useful for nodes and distant disease than for characterizing the primary tumor itself). MRI is added selectively, most often when there is concern for perineural spread or deep soft-tissue/skull-base invasion, since MRI resolves soft tissue and nerves far better than CT (the Imaging document covers this comparison in depth).

Tissue diagnosis comes from biopsy of the primary lesion or fine-needle aspiration (FNA) of a suspicious node, sometimes requiring an examination under anesthesia (EUA) for adequate sampling. Finally, every patient undergoes a set of supportive-care evaluations that matter just as much as the oncologic workup: a dental evaluation (teeth that will be in the radiation field are extracted before treatment begins, since post-radiation extractions carry a real risk of osteoradionecrosis, and fluoride treatment is started to protect the remaining teeth against radiation-related xerostomia and decay), a speech/swallow/nutrition evaluation, and smoking cessation counseling.

Subsite-Specific Workup Details

Certain subsites demand extra steps. Laryngeal cancer workup adds videostroboscopy (to assess the mucosal wave of the vocal cords, an important functional and diagnostic detail) and EUA with triple endoscopy, laryngoscopy, bronchoscopy, and esophagoscopy, both to confirm diagnosis and to screen the rest of the aerodigestive tract for synchronous disease. Oropharyngeal cancer workup places special emphasis on HPV/p16 testing, which is specifically recommended for this subsite (FNA of an involved node usually provides adequate material for testing), and diagnosis is confirmed with EUA and tonsillectomy or base-of-tongue biopsy. Nasopharyngeal cancer workup is the most distinctive: it adds EBV DNA PCR testing, since the pretreatment EBV DNA level is prognostic (higher levels correlate with worse outcomes) and can also be tracked after treatment, plus EBV testing on the tumor tissue itself (LMP immunohistochemistry or EBER in situ hybridization). Because NPC frequently extends toward the skull base and cavernous sinus, MRI of the skull base is preferred over CT for defining the primary tumor's extent and any neural involvement.

Why Oral Cavity Staging Is Different: Depth of Invasion

Most head and neck T-staging is based on tumor size and invasion of adjacent structures, but oral cavity cancer is unique in also incorporating depth of invasion (DOI), how deep the tumor has grown beneath the mucosal surface, because DOI independently predicts the risk of occult nodal metastasis and local recurrence.

T-stageOral cavity criteria
T1≤2 cm, DOI ≤5 mm
T2≤2 cm with DOI >5 mm, or 2–4 cm with DOI ≤10 mm
T32–4 cm with DOI >10 mm, or >4 cm with DOI ≤10 mm
T4a>4 cm with DOI >10 mm, or invasion of adjacent structures (mandible, maxilla, maxillary sinus, facial skin)
T4bInvasion of masticator space, pterygoid plates, or skull base, and/or carotid artery encasement

Notice that a small (≤2 cm) tumor can be upstaged from T1 to T2 purely by growing deep rather than wide, a distinction with real prognostic weight, since deeper tumors carry a higher risk of occult nodal spread (this connects directly to the Treatment Paradigms and High-Yield Literature discussions of elective neck management).

Laryngeal Staging: Vocal Cord Mobility Is the Organizing Principle

Laryngeal T-staging is organized around functional and structural landmarks rather than simple size, most importantly, vocal cord mobility. Normal mobility, impaired mobility, and fixation of the cord roughly track T1/T2, T2, and T3 disease respectively, with T3 also including invasion of the paraglottic space, pre-epiglottic space, or the inner cortex of the thyroid cartilage. T4a requires breakthrough of the outer cortex of the thyroid cartilage or extension outside the larynx, and T4b requires invasion of the prevertebral space or mediastinum, or carotid encasement. Because these criteria are largely about invasion of specific structures rather than measured size, imaging plays a central role in laryngeal staging (see the Imaging document for the CT/MRI correlates of each T-stage).

Nasopharynx: An N-Staging System Built on Location, Not Size

Nasopharyngeal carcinoma's T-staging is based on the anatomic spaces and structures invaded (parapharyngeal space, skull base, cranial nerves, and so on) rather than simple tumor diameter, fitting, since NPC grows within a tightly packed region near the skull base. More strikingly, its N-staging breaks from the pattern used everywhere else in the head and neck. Elsewhere, N-stage is built from node size, number, and laterality. In NPC, N-stage instead hinges on laterality and location relative to the caudal border of the cricoid cartilage: N1 is unilateral cervical or retropharyngeal node involvement (≤6 cm) located above the cricoid; N2 is bilateral involvement (≤6 cm), still above the cricoid; and N3 is reserved for any node, regardless of size, located below the level of the cricoid cartilage, or any node over 6 cm. This reflects the fact that in NPC, how far down the neck disease has spread predicts outcome even more than node size does.

Oropharynx: Two Staging Systems for Two Diseases

As introduced in the Epidemiology document, HPV-positive and HPV-negative oropharyngeal cancer are staged with entirely separate AJCC 8th edition systems. The HPV-positive (p16+) system uses simpler N-staging based on laterality and node count rather than extranodal extension, and its overall group-stage groupings are more favorable, reflecting the fact that a p16-positive tumor with extensive nodal disease still has a meaningfully better prognosis than an equivalent p16-negative tumor. A patient who would be stage IV under the older, HPV-negative-style criteria may be only stage I or II under the p16-positive system, even with a similar anatomic extent of disease.

Clinical PearlDepth of invasion, not just diameter, drives oral cavity T-stage, a small, deeply invasive tumor can out-stage a larger, superficial one, and DOI thresholds recur throughout oral cavity workup as triggers for considering adjuvant treatment.
Clinical PearlNasopharyngeal carcinoma is the one head and neck subsite where N-stage is about location (above vs. below the cricoid cartilage) and laterality rather than node size or number, a frequently tested exception to the general rule.

Imaging.title: Imaging in Head & Neck Cancer
Imaging.html:
Head and neck cancer relies on three imaging modalities, CT, MRI, and PET-CT, and each answers a different clinical question. Choosing the right study (or combination) at the right time is essential both for accurate staging and for designing a radiation plan that treats disease without unnecessarily irradiating normal tissue.

Matching the Modality to the Question

As a general rule: MRI gives the best soft-tissue detail and is the modality of choice when perineural spread or skull-base invasion is a concern, and for primary tumor staging in sites like the nasopharynx and oropharynx where soft-tissue extent (not bone) determines stage. CT is more accessible, faster, and remains the best modality for detecting cortical bone and cartilage erosion: which is why it is the standard for laryngeal staging, where cartilage invasion is a T-stage-defining feature. PET-CT is the modality of choice for detecting nodal and distant metastases, and it plays a unique role after treatment: because actively growing tumor is metabolically active (FDG-avid) while radiation-induced scarring and inflammation typically are not, PET-CT can help distinguish recurrent tumor from post-treatment fibrosis or neuritis: a distinction plain CT or MRI often cannot make.

Imaging the Primary Tumor by Subsite

In the oral cavity, imaging supports both staging (the anatomic boundary between the oral tongue and base of tongue is a key staging landmark) and radiation planning, since the pattern of lymphatic drainage seen on imaging directly shapes the elective nodal volume. In the oropharynx, CT typically shows an asymmetric, enhancing soft-tissue mass; as disease becomes more advanced, imaging shows loss of the normal fat planes around the tumor, signaling extension beyond the subsite of origin. In the larynx, appearance varies by compartment, supraglottic tumors appear as a soft-tissue mass with variable cartilage sclerosis and enhancement; glottic tumors appear as an exophytic or infiltrative mass on the true cord, where anterior commissure soft-tissue thickness greater than 1 mm is considered abnormal and suggests tumor extension across the midline; subglottic tumors appear as an enhancing mass at the level of the cricoid cartilage. On MRI, laryngeal tumors typically show low T1 signal, high T2/STIR signal, and variable post-contrast enhancement. In the nasopharynx, the earliest sign of tumor is often subtle, effacement of the fossa of Rosenmüller, the mucosal recess where most NPC arises, still confined by the pharyngobasilar fascia; on MRI, nasopharyngeal tumor is typically isointense to muscle on T1, iso- to hyperintense on T2, and shows heterogeneous post-contrast enhancement, with fat-saturated sequences improving detection.

Reading Lymph Nodes on Imaging

A cervical lymph node is considered suspicious for malignancy on imaging when it shows a short-axis diameter greater than 10 mm, loss of the normal fatty hilum, or cystic/necrotic change within the node. Extracapsular (extranodal) extension: tumor breaking through the node's capsule into surrounding tissue, a finding with major treatment implications, since it is one of the two definite indications for postoperative chemoradiation, is suggested by loss of the fat plane around the node, irregular capsular enhancement, and ill-defined margins.

Two nodal imaging patterns are worth memorizing because they are classic, testable pearls. First, HPV/p16-positive oropharyngeal cancer has a strong predilection for early metastasis to level II, and these metastatic nodes are frequently cystic-appearing: sometimes so much so that a cystic level II node can be the presenting finding even when the primary tumor is small or entirely occult on imaging. Second, in nasopharyngeal carcinoma, the first echelon of nodal spread is classically the retropharyngeal nodes, but skip metastasis directly to level II occurs in up to 35% of cases: meaning a clinician cannot assume the retropharyngeal nodes are involved just because level II is, or vice versa. Overall, levels II and V are the most commonly involved cervical levels in NPC.

Cartilage Invasion and the Laryngeal T-Stage Ladder

Because laryngeal T-staging is built around invasion of the cartilage framework, imaging correlates map directly onto T-stage:

StageImaging correlate
T3Vocal cord fixation, and/or paraglottic or pre-epiglottic space invasion, and/or invasion of the inner cortex of the thyroid cartilage
T4aBreakthrough of the outer cortex of the thyroid cartilage, cricoid cartilage invasion, or extralaryngeal extension (trachea, strap muscles, thyroid gland)
T4bInvasion of the prevertebral space or mediastinum, or carotid artery encasement

On CT, cartilage invasion appears as sclerosis and cortical erosion, this is why CT remains the workhorse for laryngeal staging. On MRI, invasion is inferred indirectly, most often through obliteration of the normal paraglottic fat signal.

Perineural Spread

Perineural tumor spread is a distinct entity from microscopic perineural invasion (PNI) seen only under the microscope, perineural spread is a macroscopic, radiologically visible process, most classically involving branches of the trigeminal (V) and facial (VII) nerves (including the infraorbital nerve). Classic MRI signs are nerve thickening, widening of the neural foramen it passes through, loss of the normal perineural fat, and abnormal post-contrast nerve enhancement. As with nodal recurrence, PET-CT can help separate true recurrent tumor spreading along a nerve (FDG-avid) from radiation-induced neuritis, which is typically not FDG-avid.

Clinical PearlA small or clinically occult oropharyngeal primary with a cystic level II neck node is a classic presentation of HPV-positive oropharyngeal cancer, don't mistake a cystic node for a benign process in this setting.
Clinical PearlPET-CT is especially valuable in post-treatment surveillance: recurrent or spreading tumor is FDG-avid, while radiation-induced fibrosis or neuritis typically is not, a distinction plain CT or MRI alone often cannot make.

Treatment Paradigms.title: Treatment Paradigms Across Head & Neck Subsites
Treatment Paradigms.html:
Two big questions shape treatment for almost every head and neck cancer: surgery or radiation as the primary modality, and if radiation is used, does it need concurrent chemotherapy. The answers differ by subsite, by stage, and increasingly by HPV status. This document walks through the major decision points site by site, building on a shared dosing framework used across almost all of them.

The Shared Dosing Framework

  • Definitive radiation (primary local treatment) → 70 Gy/35 fractions using a simultaneous integrated boost (SIB): 70 Gy to the gross primary tumor/involved nodes, 63 Gy to the mucosal margin and involved nodal levels, 56 Gy to the electively treated (clinically negative) neck
  • Postoperative radiation → 60 Gy/30 fractions SIB: 60 Gy to the tumor bed, 57 Gy to the rest of the operative bed, 54 Gy to the elective neck; sequential boost to 66 Gy/33 fractions for any positive margin or extracapsular extension (ECE)
  • Definitive setting, cT3–T4 or cN2+ → add concurrent cisplatin (weekly 40 mg/m², or 100 mg/m² every 3 weeks)
  • Postoperative setting, positive margin or ECE → add concurrent cisplatin
  • Cisplatin contraindicated → cetuximab or carboplatin/paclitaxel

Oral Cavity: Surgery First, Almost Always

  • Any resectable oral cavity cancer → upfront surgery, en bloc resection with negative margins, plus elective neck dissection (at least levels I–III, or I–IV for oral tongue primaries) even for a clinically node-negative neck
  • pT3–T4, pN2–3, or pT1–2/N0–1 with LVSI, PNI, close/positive margin, or DOI ≥4–5mm → adjuvant radiation
  • Positive margin or ECE → add concurrent chemotherapy
  • Inoperable (e.g., T4b) or unfit for surgery → definitive chemoradiation, or induction chemotherapy → chemoradiation

Oropharynx: Surgery vs. Radiation, and the HPV De-escalation Question

  • T1–T2 and select T3, N0–1 → transoral robotic surgery (TORS) + neck dissection
  • T3–T4, N2–N3 (or patient preference at earlier stages) → definitive radiation ± chemotherapy
  • After TORS: T3–T4, N2–N3, LVSI, PNI, or close margins → adjuvant radiation alone
  • After TORS: positive margin or ECE → adjuvant chemoradiation
  • HPV-positive disease → treated with the same intensity as HPV-negative disease, off protocol; substituting cetuximab for cisplatin produced worse survival, and dose de-escalation has failed to show noninferiority

Larynx: Organ Preservation Is the Central Question

  • Early-stage glottic, T1N0 → definitive RT, 63 Gy/28 fractions (2.25 Gy/fx)
  • Early-stage glottic, T2N0 → definitive RT, 65.25 Gy/29 fractions (2.25 Gy/fx)
  • Early-stage supraglottic/subglottic → definitive RT to 70 Gy/35 fx (concurrent chemo considered for bulky T2–T3), or larynx-preserving surgery
  • Locally advanced, functional larynx → definitive concurrent chemoradiation (organ preservation)
  • Locally advanced, non-functional larynx → total laryngectomy up front
  • Locally advanced, elective nodal coverage → levels II–IV bilaterally, level V if a node is already involved on that side, level VI if there is subglottic extension

Nasopharynx: Chemoradiation Without Surgery

  • Stage I (T1N0M0) → definitive radiation alone
  • Stage II (T2N0M0) → concurrent chemoradiation
  • Node-positive Stage II through Stage IVA → concurrent chemoradiation + induction or adjuvant chemotherapy
  • Stage IVB (metastatic), responding to initial chemo → add locoregional radiation (shown to improve survival in this setting)
  • High pretreatment EBV DNA burden → induction chemotherapy (commonly gemcitabine/cisplatin, or the TPF regimen) offers the greatest added benefit

Surgery is reserved as a salvage option for recurrence, since the tumor's deep skull-base location makes primary resection extremely difficult.

Clinical Pearl "Functional vs. non-functional larynx" is the single question that separates definitive chemoradiation from upfront total laryngectomy in locally advanced disease. It is a functional judgment, not purely a staging one.
Clinical Pearl Despite its dramatically better prognosis, HPV-positive oropharyngeal cancer is, for now, treated with the same intensity as HPV-negative disease outside of a clinical trial. Multiple de-escalation strategies (cetuximab substitution, dose reduction) have been tested and have so far failed to show they are safe.

High-Yield Literature.title: High-Yield Practice-Changing Trials in Head & Neck Cancer
High-Yield Literature.html:
Head and neck oncology has been shaped by a relatively small set of landmark trials, and knowing not just their names but why each one changed practice is what separates rote memorization from real understanding. This document walks through the trials that define today's standards of care.

Establishing Chemotherapy's Role: MACH-NC

The MACH-NC meta-analysis (Pignon et al.) pooled patient-level data from over 17,000 patients across 93 trials, an enormous sample that could detect benefits too small for any single trial to prove reliably. It found that adding chemotherapy to radiation produced a 4.5% absolute overall survival benefit at 5 years, but the benefit was not uniform: concurrent chemoradiation carried a significant 6.5% OS benefit, while induction chemotherapy's 2.4% benefit did not reach significance, and patients over age 70 did not benefit at all. This is the single piece of evidence most responsible for cementing concurrent chemoradiation, rather than induction chemotherapy, as the preferred way to combine radiation and systemic therapy for locally advanced disease.

Defining Adjuvant ChemoRT: RTOG 9501 and EORTC 22931

Once surgery is done, when should chemotherapy be added to postoperative radiation? Two parallel trials answered this. RTOG 9501 (Cooper et al.) randomized patients with high-risk features (≥2 positive nodes, ECE, or positive margins) after surgery to radiation alone versus radiation plus concurrent cisplatin; the overall trial showed improved locoregional control but no OS difference, but an unplanned subset analysis restricted to patients with positive margins and/or ECE showed a real benefit in locoregional failure and disease-free survival. EORTC 22931 (Bernier et al.), using broader high-risk criteria (T3–T4, N2–N3, or any of +margin/ECE/PNI/vascular invasion), found that chemoradiation significantly improved both PFS and OS. When the two trials were pooled, only ECE and/or microscopically positive margins emerged as risk factors with a consistent, significant benefit from adding chemotherapy across both datasets, which is exactly why ECE and positive margins are the two definite (NCCN category 1) indications for postoperative chemoradiation today, while other risk factors (multiple positive nodes, PNI, LVSI, pT3–T4) are only "additional factors to consider."

The Cisplatin Dosing Debate: Weekly vs. Every 3 Weeks

Concurrent cisplatin was traditionally given at 100 mg/m² every 3 weeks, but this dose causes substantial toxicity, prompting interest in a lower weekly dose. A large VA retrospective study (Bauml et al., ~2,900 patients) found that high-dose (100 mg/m² q3wk) cisplatin was not associated with improved OS compared to low-dose weekly (40 mg/m²) cisplatin, but was associated with more acute kidney injury, neutropenia, dehydration, and hearing loss. A subsequent Indian phase III RCT (Noronha et al.) tested an even lower weekly dose (30 mg/m²) against the traditional 100 mg/m² q3-week regimen and found the higher dose gave better 2-year locoregional control (though not significantly better OS) at the cost of more grade 3+ toxicity, showing that 30 mg/m² weekly is too low. Taken together, this evidence base is why 40 mg/m² weekly cisplatin is a widely used, lower-toxicity alternative to the historical 100 mg/m² q3-week regimen, even though the higher dose remains NCCN category 1.

Targeted Therapy: Bonner's Early Promise and Cetuximab's Later Disappointment

The Bonner trial tested cetuximab (an EGFR-targeting antibody with a different, generally milder toxicity profile than cisplatin) added to definitive radiation in stage III–IV HNSCC, and found a substantial median OS improvement (49 vs. 29 months), with the largest benefit concentrated in oropharyngeal cancer patients specifically, while larynx and hypopharynx patients saw little benefit. This established cetuximab plus radiation as an option, particularly for patients who cannot tolerate cisplatin. But when researchers later tried to use cetuximab as a less-toxic substitute for cisplatin specifically in good-prognosis HPV-positive oropharyngeal cancer, hoping to preserve cure rates while reducing side effects, both RTOG 1016 and De-ESCALaTE HPV found the opposite of what was hoped: cetuximab substitution produced significantly worse OS and/or higher recurrence than cisplatin, with no meaningful reduction in toxicity. The lesson these two trial generations teach together: cetuximab is a reasonable option when cisplatin truly cannot be given, but it is not a "safer swap" for cisplatin in patients who can tolerate it.

Larynx Preservation: The VA Larynx Study and RTOG 91-11

Before the 1990s, total laryngectomy was standard for locally advanced laryngeal cancer. The VA Larynx Study tested whether induction chemotherapy followed by radiation (in responders) could preserve the larynx without compromising survival, compared to upfront surgery, it found no difference in overall survival between the two approaches, with a 64% larynx preservation rate in the chemotherapy-first arm. This was the trial that first proved organ preservation was oncologically safe. RTOG 91-11 then asked a more refined question: among non-surgical approaches, which is best, induction chemotherapy then radiation, concurrent chemoradiation, or radiation alone? Concurrent chemoradiation won decisively, with significantly better long-term larynx preservation (82% vs. 64% for radiation alone) and local control than the other two arms, and again no significant OS difference between arms. Together, these two trials are why concurrent chemoradiation, not induction chemotherapy or radiation alone, is the standard organ-preservation approach for locally advanced laryngeal cancer with a functional larynx today.

Nodal Management in Oral Cavity: Tata Memorial and Senti-MERORL

For clinically node-negative (cN0) early oral cavity cancer, should the neck be treated electively or only if a node later becomes apparent? The Tata Memorial trial (D'Cruz et al.) randomized T1–T2 cN0 patients to elective ipsilateral neck dissection versus watchful waiting with dissection only at relapse, and found elective dissection significantly improved both overall survival (80% vs. 67.5% at 3 years) and disease-free survival, establishing elective neck dissection as standard even when the neck looks clinically clear. A separate question is how much of the neck needs to be removed electively; the Senti-MERORL trial tested whether sentinel lymph node biopsy, with full dissection performed only if the sentinel node is positive, could achieve equivalent oncologic outcomes to upfront full dissection while sparing morbidity, it found equivalent 2-year neck recurrence-free survival between the two strategies, with significantly better functional outcomes in the sentinel-node arm, supporting sentinel node biopsy as a standard option for early-stage disease.

HPV Rewrites the Prognosis Model: RTOG 0129

A retrospective analysis of the RTOG 0129 trial (Ang et al.), originally designed to compare fractionation schedules, became one of the most influential papers in the field when it showed that HPV/p16 status was a far stronger predictor of survival than the fractionation schedule being tested: 3-year OS was roughly 82–84% in HPV/p16-positive patients versus only 51–57% in HPV/p16-negative patients. This analysis produced a risk-stratification nomogram (based on p16 status, smoking pack-years, and T/N stage) and is the single piece of evidence most responsible for the entire subsequent wave of HPV-driven staging changes and de-escalation research described elsewhere in these documents.

Confirming Chemotherapy's Benefit in Nasopharyngeal Cancer

Intergroup 0099 randomized T3–T4 or node-positive NPC patients to radiation alone versus radiation with concurrent and adjuvant cisplatin-based chemotherapy, and found such a large survival advantage with chemotherapy (5-year OS 67% vs. 37%) that the trial was stopped early because continuing to withhold chemotherapy from the control arm was no longer considered ethical. The MAC-NPC meta-analysis (Blanchard et al., 7,080 patients across 26 trials) later confirmed this signal at scale, finding that adding concurrent chemotherapy produced the largest OS benefit of any chemotherapy strategy tested, with additional (smaller) benefit from adding induction or adjuvant chemotherapy on top of concurrent chemoradiation, translating to roughly a 6% absolute OS benefit at 5 years and 8% at 10 years.

Clinical PearlWhen a "less toxic" substitute for cisplatin is tested (cetuximab in RTOG 1016/De-ESCALaTE, lower cisplatin doses in the Indian RCT), the recurring lesson is that toxicity and efficacy don't always trade off cleanly, several attempted substitutions turned out to sacrifice cancer control without meaningfully reducing side effects.
Clinical PearlRTOG 91-11's primary endpoint was laryngectomy-free survival, not overall survival, a good reminder that a trial's chosen endpoint shapes what "winning" means; concurrent chemoRT won on local control and larynx preservation despite showing no OS advantage over the other arms.
